NextItNet supports causal dilated convolutions with residual blocks for short- and long-range dependencies; its reported residual-block comparison supports residual learning, not a recent-context gate specifically. [Original paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf). Mechanistically, h′ₜ=hₜ+g(cₜ)⊙F(h)ₜ scales the complete residual update while preserving the identity shortcut. A recent-context gate conditions transformation strength on recent activity; it does not explicitly weight historical positions or guarantee monotonically stronger recency. Earlier blocks can already mix older information into hₜ. Any recency claim therefore needs measured temporal influence.

Suggested ablations: unchanged baseline; fixed residual scale matched to average gate magnitude; learned context-independent scalar/channel scales; adaptive recent-context gate; explicit lag-decay or truncated-context control. Train each independently under the same seed, budget and pinned validation protocol. Compare macro HR@10, gate variability, and prediction changes after perturbing older versus recent history. Gains over constant scaling support context dependence; altered lag sensitivity supports temporal reweighting. Gate magnitudes alone establish neither. These are proposed controls, not published evidence for this exact gate.

To preserve baseline h+F(h), initialize the multiplier to one. For a plain sigmoid gate, zero weights/bias produce 0.5 and halve the residual; bias logit(0.99)≈4.60 approximates baseline but reduces gate gradients. An exact alternative is g=2σ(Wc+b), with W=b=0: initial g=1, unchanged shortcut, and room to learn suppression or amplification. These initialization conclusions follow algebraically. [ReZero](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04887) provides evidence for zero-initialized residual scaling as an optimization strategy, but that starts blocks at identity h, not the existing NextItNet behavior h+F(h); it supplies no evidence of recency weighting.
